topic.title: Only paying the minimum on your credit card: what it really costs you

title: Only paying the minimum on a $5,000 card? Here is the real cost
description:
Rohan owes $5,000 on his credit card and pays the minimum, on time, every month. It feels responsible. We follow that balance down a long road and compute how many years it really takes and what it costs in total.
Then the same balance with one fixed payment that clears it in three years, the two roads side by side.
And the line on a US card statement that already shows you the fix.

lines.text: Minimum due, $150. Rohan pays it, on time, every month. Keep that up, and his balance of $5,000 costs him $11,638.
Wait. I never miss a payment. How can it cost that much?
Because at that pace, every dinner and every gadget on this card ends up costing about 2.3× its price.
And he is far from alone. Millions of people do exactly this. The bill is paid, nothing is late, and it feels responsible.
So in the next few minutes: how long the minimum really takes, how much it really costs, and the one line on your statement that fixes it.
Paying the minimum is like running on a treadmill, Rohan. You work hard every month, and the belt keeps pulling you back.
The belt is interest. His card charges 1.85% a month on whatever he still owes.
That sounds small. But over a year it adds up to 22.2%. And because interest is charged on interest, it really works out to about 25%.
Okay, but I pay $150 every single month. That has to add up to something.
Here is how that minimum is worked out. It is a small slice of the balance, 3% on this card. Owed, $5,000. Minimum, $150.
So he pays. Then interest lands on everything that is left, and a big part of his payment simply leaks back out as next month's interest.
Now the sneaky part. As the balance shrinks, the minimum shrinks with it. His steps get smaller, right when he should be speeding up.
The minimum is not built to get you out. It is built to keep you in.
Twelve months go by. Rohan pays the minimum every single time. Never late, not once.
By now, he has paid $1,685. And he still owes $4,323.
I paid all that, and I still owe that much?
Because $1,008 of what he paid went straight to the bank as interest. Only the rest touched the actual debt.
And Rohan? That was the good year.
From here, the road gets long. A new year, a new signpost, and the balance is still walking right beside him.
Here is the whole journey if he keeps paying only the minimum. Red is what he still owes. Green is everything he has paid.
Look how the red line flattens out. The smaller the balance, the smaller the minimum, so the last stretch drags on for years.
In total, it takes 199 monthly payments. That is about 17 years.
Years? I will be paying this off longer than I have been working!
By the time this card is cleared, Rohan could change jobs, move cities, maybe start a family. And still be paying for this year's shopping.
All in, he pays $11,638 to clear $5,000. And $6,638 of that is pure interest.
In my bank days, we had a name for people who paid only the minimum. Our best customers. They never complained, and they never left.
And our maths is the kind version. Real cards charge interest daily, on the balance before your payment lands. And keep using the card, and new purchases charge interest from day one.
So the real bill is even bigger?
Usually, yes. So stop playing their game. Change one rule.
Same card. Same $5,000. Same rate. One change. Instead of the minimum, Rohan picks one fixed payment, and never lets it shrink.
To clear the whole balance in three years, that payment is $191 a month.
His very first minimum was $150. The fixed payment is $191. A bigger step, but not a giant leap.
That's it? I can find that.
The trick is that it never shrinks. Same big step on the treadmill every month, while the belt keeps slowing down.
As the balance falls, interest has less to chew on. So more of every payment hits the debt, and the debt falls faster and faster.
36 payments. And then it is gone.
Now the two roads, side by side. Minimum only: about 17 years, and $6,638 in interest. The fixed payment: three years, and $1,893.
Same debt, same rate. The minimum road costs $11,638 in total. The fixed road, $6,893.
Years sooner, and thousands less? Why did nobody tell me?
Somebody did. It is printed on your statement, every single month.
In the US, card statements carry a minimum payment warning. It shows how long you will be paying if you pay only the minimum, and what it will cost in total.
For a balance like this one, there is a second line. The monthly payment that clears it in three years, and what that would cost.
That number is the fix. No calculator needed. The card company has already done the maths for you.
Found it. It has been sitting there every month.
One. Find the three year payment on the statement, and set autopay for that amount. Not the minimum.
Two. Stop adding new spending to this card while he clears it. Otherwise the belt speeds up again.
Three. In a good month, pay a little extra. Every extra dollar goes straight at the balance.
One honest catch. If even that payment does not fit the budget, keep paying at least the minimum. A missed payment brings late fees, and can push the rate even higher.
And then pick up the phone. Ask the card company for a lower rate or a payment plan. Asking costs nothing.
So, two roads. Minimum only: about 17 years and $11,638. One fixed payment: 36 months and $6,893.
Autopay set. Fixed payment, not the minimum. And for the first time, this card has a finish line.
Our maths is simplified, so real cards usually cost a bit more. Follow the panchayat for one money question, settled with real maths.
